problem.heading: The problem
problem.title: One missing element, and the statement of claim is rejected on form before a judge reads the merits.
problem.body: Every civil case in Algeria starts with the statement of claim. The Code of Civil and Administrative Procedure lists what it must contain; miss one element and the court rules it inadmissible on form. Lawyers draft it by hand, and they cannot send a client's file to a cloud AI service.

story.title: Nine steps, and every mandatory element is checked by code, not by AI.
story.lead: The case fills in step by step, and the statement of claim takes shape on paper in front of you. The formal check points at the missing element at once and names the article that requires it. When the AI drafts the legal grounds, the sheet shows which lines the code quoted and which the model wrote, and the lawyer ticks the review box before anything is exported.
story.missing: One mandatory element missing: the statement of claim risks being declared inadmissible on form.
story.present: Every mandatory element the app checks is present. That does not make the claim admissible: substance, jurisdiction and time limits remain the lawyer's call.
story.caption: As the workbench shows it: the formal state changes with every letter you type, and the legal grounds carry the AI mark until the lawyer has reviewed them.

dl.title: The desktop app for Windows
dl.lead: The product lawyers use. It runs offline on your own computer: client files never leave it, and the AI, when you want it, runs locally too.
dl.steps.title: Install in three steps
dl.step1: Download the zip from the latest release.
dl.step2: Unzip it into any folder. No installer: the folder holds everything.
dl.step3: Run DzLegalAssistant.exe. On first launch: a welcome screen, then a three-step setup (the lawyer, the office, preferences) that fills the signature block of every new statement of claim, then the start screen.
dl.step4: Without an AI model, choose the engine “Without AI (fill-in templates)”: the form, the formal check, the law library and the exports all work.
dl.req.title: Requirements
dl.req.runtime: No .NET to install: the package carries its runtime, the legal texts and the fonts.
dl.req.memory: Without AI: any recent computer. With the local model: 8 GB of memory at least (gemma3:4b), 16 GB recommended.
dl.ai.title: The local AI model, optional
dl.ai.body: The model reads the facts, proposes the claim type and the articles, then writes the legal grounds. It runs on your computer through Ollama. Neither is bundled with the app: you install them under their own terms.
dl.ai.step1: Install Ollama. It runs as a local process at 127.0.0.1:11434.
dl.ai.step2: Run ollama pull gemma3:4b (about 3.3 GB, a one-time download). After that, no network is needed.
dl.ai.step3: The app looks for Ollama at start-up and every 30 seconds, and says plainly when it is not running or the model is not installed.
dl.ai.speed: On an ordinary laptop without a graphics card (Intel i5-1335U), the live recording shows 3 min 17 s to read the facts and 2 min 33 s to draft the grounds. The first request after start-up also loads the model (10 to 40 s).

law.honest.title: Limits, stated plainly
law.honest.1: No practising lawyer has verified the legal rules and the catalogue yet. An independent audit in October 2026 found errors in the catalogue; corrections are under way.
law.honest.2: The Civil, Commercial and Labour codes are only partly loaded, with the articles the app's claim types rely on. The complete Civil Code is being checked against the Official Journal.
law.honest.3: Repealed articles are not included; the text loaded is the one in force today.
law.inApp: In the app, the law library shows these same texts with a search by article number or word, a copy button and a link to the official source of each text.
privacy.lead2: Client case data is covered by professional secrecy. The desktop app is built so that no case data leaves the lawyer's computer.
privacy.network.title: What the desktop app does on the network
privacy.row3.n: HTTP to 127.0.0.1:11434 only: a conversation with the Ollama process on the same computer. Packets never leave the machine.
privacy.row4.c: Grounds suggestions, law library, article search
privacy.row4.n: None. The texts and the claim catalogue ship with the app.
privacy.row5.n: None by the app itself. When you click one, the operating system opens it in your browser; the link is fixed data, never built from case content.
privacy.row6.c: Telemetry, analytics, crash reports, update checks
privacy.enforced.title: How the code enforces it
privacy.enforced.1: The model client accepts only literal loopback addresses (127.0.0.0/8, ::1, localhost). Any other host is refused without even a DNS lookup.
privacy.enforced.2: That client uses no proxy, follows no redirect, and opens every connection itself to a loopback address, whatever host a request names.
privacy.enforced.3: Ollama “cloud” models, which would forward prompts to ollama.com, are refused.
privacy.enforced.4: The hosted-model code of the web demo lives in a separate project the desktop app does not reference; a test fails the build if it ever does, and publishing with the online testing flag fails too.
privacy.enforced.5: The running app sends no telemetry. Automated tests cover the guard and a full draft-and-check loop with no network.
privacy.verify.title: Verify it yourself
privacy.verify.1: Disconnect the computer from every network, or disable the adapter.
privacy.verify.2: Start the app and use template mode. Everything works.
privacy.verify.3: With Ollama installed and the model pulled beforehand, the local model works too, because Ollama itself runs locally.
privacy.verify.4: Watch the connections if you like (netstat -ano on Windows): the only one is to 127.0.0.1:11434.
privacy.storage.title: Where data is stored
privacy.storage.1: Drafts are saved where you choose; the default folder is {0}.
privacy.storage.3: The lawyer's profile from the first-run setup is stored on this computer only and never sent anywhere.
privacy.storage.4: A recovery copy is kept while you work; after an unexpected close, the app offers to resume. Nothing is synchronised.
privacy.demo.title: The web demo is different
privacy.demo.lead: The public demo at /app is a separate program for trying the product from a link. The one difference is where the AI runs.
privacy.demo.1: What you type is sent to a hosted model (Nemotron 3 Ultra through OpenRouter, with Google AI Studio and Groq as fallbacks). Enter fictitious cases only.
privacy.demo.2: The server keeps no account and stores no case. Your case is kept as a recovery copy in your own browser for at most a day; “Clear browser copy” deletes it at once.
privacy.demo.3: AI calls are limited per browser session and per network address (60 and 150 an hour); the address is used for that count.
privacy.demo.4: The app bar says “Demo · fictitious cases only”, and the page carries noindex.
privacy.demo.5: The demo also sets the framework's standard security cookie (its name starts with .AspNetCore.Antiforgery), which holds no case data.
privacy.site.title: This website
privacy.site.1: Static pages served from the same address as the demo. No analytics, no tracking, nothing loaded from another origin.
privacy.site.2: Two first-party cookies, written only when you choose a language or a theme (dzlegal.lang, dzlegal.theme), kept for a year.
privacy.site.3: The fonts and icons are bundled with their licences; the page's security policy allows no inline scripts and no framing.
privacy.site.4: The Windows download (served by GitHub) and the links to the Official Journal (joradp.dz) leave this site; they are plain links, loaded only when you click them.
about.what.title: What it does, and does not do
about.what.decide: The app drafts; it does not decide. It does not judge the merits or guarantee a result, and the lawyer reviews and signs every statement of claim.
about.team.did.lead: Defined the product and its legal pipeline, directed and reviewed the AI coding agents that wrote most of the code, ran the benchmarks and the test campaigns, and tested the app.
about.team.did.design: Designed and built the lawyer's journey in the desktop app: the welcome screen, the setup, the lawyer's profile, the start screen, the guided tour with its sample case, the help pages and the law library, in Arabic and English, light and dark.
about.team.did.legal: Master's in private law, works in an Algerian law office. Reviewed legal points of the drafting and answered the team's questions on Algerian civil procedure and claim types, which shaped the family claims.
about.built.title: How it was built
about.built.ai: Most of the code, tests and documentation were written by AI coding agents, directed and reviewed by the team: Claude Code (most of the app), OpenAI Codex (the law corpus, part of the workbench, the independent test cases) and OpenCode (the onboarding screens). The welcome image was generated with ChatGPT. Inside the desktop app, the only AI is the local model (Gemma 3 4B through Ollama); the web demo uses Nemotron 3 Ultra through OpenRouter.
about.built.stack.title: Tech stack
about.built.stack: C# and .NET 10; Avalonia (desktop interface); Blazor Server (web demo); QuestPDF (PDF) and Open XML SDK (Word); Scriban (templates); Ollama (local model); OpenRouter (the web demo's hosted model).

about.status.title: Status and limits
about.status.1: The legal rules and the claim catalogue are not yet verified by a practising lawyer. Every rule is marked unverified in the data and in the app; an independent audit in October 2026 found errors in the catalogue, and corrections are under way.
about.status.2: One document type so far: the statement of claim. The Civil, Commercial and Labour codes are only partly loaded.
about.status.3: The web demo sends what is typed to a hosted model: fictitious cases only. The desktop app sends nothing.
about.status.4: The local model is the weak point today: slower and less precise than the online model. The desktop app stays offline by default; an online mode will be the lawyer's choice, case by case.
about.next.title: What is next
about.next.lead: The plan, as written in the repository:
about.next.1: Month 1: an online mode for stronger AI, with client names hidden on the laptop before sending and a preview of exactly what is sent; executable legal rules reviewed with the legal reviewer.
about.next.2: Month 2: version 1.0 as a Windows installer, with the complete Civil Code and the texts reviewed by a practising lawyer.
about.next.3: Month 3: a pilot in five to ten law offices, measuring the time saved and the defects caught.
meta.try.description: Five steps to test DZ Legal Assistant in the live demo: open a sample, watch the formal check, analyse the facts, draft the grounds, export before and after the review.
try.title: Test it in 5 minutes
try.lead: Five steps in the live demo, with what to click, what you should see and why it matters for a lawyer. The demo runs the same screens as the desktop app, with a hosted model: fictitious data only.
try.step1.title: Open the sample {0}
try.step1.click: In the top bar, open {0} and choose {1}.
try.step1.expect: The nine steps of {0} fill in, the statement of claim appears on paper under {1}, and {2} shows 8 / 9: every element is present except the legal grounds, not drafted yet.
try.step1.time: A few seconds. Nothing is sent to the AI.
try.step1.why: The form, the paper and the check are one object: every element the Code requires is tracked from the first keystroke.
try.step2.title: Clear the defendant's address
try.step2.click: Open the Defendant step, clear the domicile field, and look at {0}.
try.step2.expect: The score drops to 7 / 9 and a red card names the defendant's domicile and cites CPCA art. 15-3. The formal check does not block {0}: the lawyer decides, and the card stays until the address is back. Put it back: 8 / 9 again.
try.step2.why: A statement of claim missing one mandatory element can be declared inadmissible on form before any judge reads it. This check is code, not AI, and works the same offline.
try.step3.click: Open the Legal grounds step and press {0}.
try.step3.expect: The AI's reading of the facts (the legal relationship, the obligation breached, what is sought) and the question “Is this the type of claim?”. Nothing is ticked until you press {0}; then the articles this claim rests on are ticked, each with its official text and its source.
try.step3.time: In the 31 October 2026 hidden-set run, the online model read a case in 8 s on average; the activity panel shows a timer.
try.step3.why: The lawyer confirms the legal qualification before any article is used.
try.step4.expect: The Legal grounds section is written: the program quotes each ticked article's rule from the official text, the AI writes how the facts meet it. The section is marked {0} with the box {1} under it. Paragraphs that fail the checks (a number not in the facts, law the lawyer did not give) are flagged or removed, and an amber note says what happened.
try.step4.time: The activity panel shows the elapsed time. No published measurement exists for the hosted model's drafting time, so none is promised here.
try.step4.why: The rule comes from the official text and the AI only applies it; the lawyer reviews every AI-written line.
try.step5.title: Export before and after the review
try.step5.click: Press {0} before ticking the box. Then tick {1} and press {0} again.
try.step5.expect: First, {0} lists the unreviewed AI section and nothing downloads. After the tick, the PDF downloads ({1} works the same way); {2} shows the pages first if you like.
try.step5.why: No statement of claim leaves the app with an unreviewed AI section: the lawyer signs.
try.note.title: Before you start
try.note.1: The first visit can take up to a minute: the free server wakes up on demand, and the page says so while it loads.
try.note.2: Fictitious data only. What you type is sent to a hosted model; the four sample cases are invented.
try.note.3: AI calls are limited: 60 per browser session and 150 per network address an hour. The formal check, editing and export are not limited.
try.same: The demo's own guide ({0} in its top bar) takes you through the same five steps: it lights up the field or button to use next, never presses it for you, and moves on once you have done the step.
try.cta: Open the demo with its guide
